I have sat in rooms where the most important things in human life were reduced to a line item and then cut. Twenty years in healthcare taught me what it costs when systems stop seeing people. The moment someone stopped producing, the system stopped knowing what to do with them.

The world is in transition. The climate is destabilizing. Political systems are fracturing. Geopolitical orders are shifting. Technology is remaking what it means to work, to know, to connect. Every system we built in the last century is being stress-tested at once. And through all of it, the same question keeps getting skipped: what does it mean to be human, right now, in a world that is changing faster than we can make sense of it?

That is not a philosophical question. I believe it is a design challenge. And it is the most urgent one I know.

I work at the intersection of systemic thinking, evaluative inquiry, and relational practice. My work is not about teaching frameworks or delivering (expert) answers — it is about creating the conditions under which people and organisations become more capable of asking better questions, sitting with uncertainty, and learning their way toward something new. Even innovative.



I design and I hold spaces — in conferences, organisations, and communities of practice — where genuine inquiry can happen: where the relational and the analytical meet, where self-awareness and collective sense-making reinforce each other, and where the aspiration to do things differently has room to take form. Drawing on systems thinking, the Process Enneagram work by Richard Knowles, and a long practice of working across the science-policy interface, I bring intellectual rigour and personal warmth to encounters that are meant to disturb as much as they are meant to support.

As AI systems evolve, I want to preserve the core principles of accountability, traceability, and clarity that underpin traditional regulatory and auditing practices.

In regulated environments, systems are not trusted because they are advanced. They are trusted because their behavior can be documented, explained, and verified. That standard should not be lost as AI introduces more adaptive and probabilistic technologies.

I am committed to conserving the expectation that outcomes must be attributable, that decisions can be traced back to inputs and processes, and that responsibility remains clearly defined. Even as AI systems become more complex, organizations must retain the ability to answer fundamental questions: What happened, why did it happen, and who is accountable?

I want to conserve the idea of stewardship and responsibility even as technology accelerates to prevent real world harm.

A good collaborative relationship is built on clarity, accountability, and the ability to engage in direct, honest dialogue without losing alignment on shared goals.

In my experience, especially as a Director of Operations, collaboration is most effective when roles, expectations, and decision boundaries are clearly defined from the outset. This reduces ambiguity and prevents gaps in ownership, which are common sources of failure in both technical and organizational systems.

Equally important is the ability to challenge ideas constructively. Strong collaboration requires participants to question assumptions, surface risks, and address disagreements directly, rather than avoiding them. This is especially critical in my work, where unexamined assumptions can lead to downstream failures.

At the same time, collaboration must remain outcome-focused. Productive teams maintain alignment on the objective, even when perspectives differ. This allows for diverse expertise to contribute meaningfully without fragmenting the direction of the work.

Finally, trust is built through consistency: following through on commitments, communicating transparently, and documenting decisions so they can be revisited and understood over time.

I am committed to this domain because current AI deployment practices do not adequately account for how humans actually interact with these systems in real-world environments.

In regulated industries, we already understand that outcomes are not determined by systems alone, but by the interaction between systems, processes, and people. However, most AI governance approaches still treat the isolated model as the primary risk surface, while overlooking the human–AI interface where failures most often occur.

Through my work in quality control, regulatory compliance, and auditing, I have repeatedly seen that breakdowns are rarely caused by a single component failing in isolation. They emerge from misalignment of the system as a whole: miscommunication, misuse, or misunderstanding between human operators and the systems they rely on. AI systems amplify this risk because they are probabilistic, adaptive, and often opaque to end users.

This gap creates a critical need for frameworks that can evaluate not only system performance, but also how human interaction shapes outcomes over time. My work focuses on addressing this gap by integrating traditional auditing principles with human-in-the-loop analysis and AI literacy.

text.content:
I believe every person has the right to shape their own life. Progress cannot happen to people  it must happen with them. When a circular economy decides what gets measured, what gets celebrated, and whose costs are acceptable, without the participation of all affected actors, it doesn't distribute progress. It distributes its burdens downward while its benefits rise upward.
That is the invisible harm I want to make visible.
What I want to conserve is the integrity of honest accounting the courage to ask what we are not counting, and why. Every metric enshrines a value judgement. A lifecycle assessment that ignores the health burden on communities near green recycling facilities is not measuring circularity. It is measuring only the part those with power have decided is worth seeing.
I also want to conserve shared accountability. A truly circular economy cannot be circular only in its materials  it must be circular in its responsibility. Those who design these systems must answer to those who live within them.
Most of all, I want to conserve the question itself: who benefits, and who bears the cost? That question becomes unwelcome as systems mature and interests consolidate. I want to keep asking it  because the deepest harm any system causes is the harm it causes while believing itself to be good.

I believe human progress is only meaningful when it preserves the freedom of every person to shape their own life. That conviction is at the heart of my concern with the circular economy.
The circular economy decides what counts as progress  what gets measured, what gets celebrated, and crucially, what gets ignored. But those decisions are not neutral. When a system is designed without the participation of all actors it affects, it doesn't distribute progress  it distributes its costs downward while its benefits flow upward. The burdens land on communities that had no seat at the table where the metrics were chosen.
That is the invisible harm I am trying to make visible. Not an accident of poor design, but a structural consequence of who gets to define what circularity means and who it is meant to serve.
My research is driven by a simple but urgent belief that a truly circular economy cannot be circular only in its materials. It must also be circular in its accountability. Progress, if it is to mean anything at all, must be a shared responsibility toward every actor in the system  not a profit that rises while the burden sinks.

text.content:
I am a design researcher and that distinction matters. I don't only study broken systems; I build interventions that can shift them over time. My work sits at the intersection of environmental justice and systems thinking, approached through the lens of a designer who is drawn to wicked challenges precisely because they resist easy solutions.
Much of what I do is about capacity building working with individuals and communities who have been absorbing the consequences of inequitable systems without ever being invited to redesign them. I believe people closest to the harm hold the clearest understanding of what needs to change. My role is to help them translate that understanding into agency.
I am a risk taker. I choose research questions that are inconvenient, that implicate powerful systems, and that don't resolve neatly. The circular economy's invisible harms is one such question  sitting uncomfortably at the edge of what the field is willing to examine about itself.
I bring a rare combination: the rigour of academic research, the practice of design, and a long commitment to justice work on the ground. I am looking for mentors who can help me sharpen that combination thinkers who are unafraid of complexity, who value interdisciplinary work, and who believe research must ultimately serve the people it studies.

This topic became personally meaningful to me through my experience as a college student moving in and out of dormitories each semester. I noticed how many usable objects, furniture, and personal items are often discarded simply because students cannot transport them or find someone to reuse them. Many of these items end up in dumpsters even though they still have value.

Seeing this pattern made me realize how everyday design systems encourage short lifespans and constant replacement, especially for people who are temporarily living in a place such as international or study abroad students. This observation led me to think about the larger system behind waste: how design decisions, economic systems, and social behaviors reinforce a cycle of consumption and disposal.

As a architecture student I had constantly seen how material are constantly being use in a wasteful manner because of these experiences, I feel a strong responsibility as a future designer and architect to rethink how products, buildings, and systems are created so they can support reuse, adaptability, and long term sustainability rather than contributing to waste.

text.content: My interest in this domain comes from seeing how migration decisions are shaped by both structural demand for labor and personal aspirations for stability. Transnational labor systems in care and agriculture are essential to economies, yet they can place workers in positions where opportunity and vulnerability coexist. I’m interested in examining these systems because they affect families, remittance flows, and long-term life trajectories. My concern is with how recruitment pathways, visa structures, and labor demand interact to produce conditions that can either support or constrain worker agency. For me, understanding this domain is important because it offers a way to think about how essential labor systems might be structured more equitably while still meeting global workforce needs.

Transnational labor systems in care and agriculture are essential to economies, yet they can place workers in positions where opportunity and vulnerability coexist. I’m interested in examining these systems because they affect families, remittance flows, and long-term life trajectories. My concern is with how recruitment pathways, visa structures, and labor demand interact to produce conditions that can either support or constrain worker agency. For me, understanding this domain is important because it offers a way to think about how essential labor systems might be structured more equitably while still meeting global workforce needs.

I came to recognize and care about this domain for two reasons:

Firstly, I increasingly perceive the world to be filled with perverse attractor states: attractor states resulting from addictive cycles which offer diminishing utility as people fall more deeply into them. I think it's important to acknowledge the utility of these states, and also to normalize the field a bit such that the attractor states are divets, or even pitholes, rather than chasms. I think the issue is less that the problems exist-- because problems/challenges offer opportunity for growth-- and is moreso problematic because of the addictive & nigh unescapable nature of the problems if a person wishes to retain the utility which the solution offers. (examples: algorithmic echo chambers; social media optimized for engagement; etc)

The second reason is because I have ADHD, and have always needed different cognitive support than my peers. I was always intellectually capable, but struggle/d with simpler things such as memory & executive function, and I found joy in the necessity of building my own tools & systems. I find that we assume a one-size-fits all solution to cognitive enhancement due to needing to serve economies of scale, and I think there's lots of room for new answers to this problem with AI.

text.content:
The core of this domain explores the development of the internet and social platforms from their origins to today. The transformation from non-curated collections of human expression into billion dollar industries that utilize algorithmic tools trained on user data to predict and control future behavior.

These tools not only automate information flows about us, but automate us. This theory comes primarily from "The Age of Surveillance Capitalism" by Shoshana Zuboff which I have been diving into recently, which argues that these tools do not merely automate information flows about us, but that they automate us. One thing she emphasizes is the "unprecedented" nature of surveillance capitalism, how humans have a habit of understanding the new through the familiar: the first cars were called "horseless carriages," taking old terms and using them to describe something new. She argues that that is what we are doing with surveillance capitalism, using existing vocabulary around privacy, monopoly, and regulation which were created to describe a different world, this leads us to pursuing inadequate interventions.

Zuboff reframes the user in the system, arguing that the user is not the product itself, but the source material. Extraction from that source happens well before we see the product. Crucially the behavioral surplus isn't simply observed, but it is altered and manipulated. Every interface decision, every engagement mechanic, every notification is designed to generate richer and more predictable data. The customer is not the user, it is really the companies purchasing predictions about our future behavior.

How do we return agency to the user, and is it possible to build a mutual transaction between users and the platforms they inhabit? What does agency even mean inside a system designed to predict and shape behavior? What would structural change actually require?

text.content: As someone who has grown up online this domain is personally uncomfortable, but in a good way. The more I have read into surveillance capitalism the harder it has become to unsee in my everyday use of social media and tools online. The online environments I have been conditioned to believe are "normal", like social feeds, recommendation engines, search results, are not neutral tools. They are designed to extract, predict, and nudge me as a user. I am concerned about how social platforms flatten creative expression to what is algorithmically rewarded, and how politics are filtered through engagement logic rather than truth or relevance. I believe recognizing the modern internet as the unprecedented technology is the first step to imagining something different.

text.content: Since I study the use of generative AI, I’d like to clarify that I do not feel techno-utopian or techno-fatalist about it. Simultaneously, I do feel an obligation to study this technology and its impact on people. From my research, I see that 1) students are currently using this technology and that it is impacting their education and 2) instructors are struggling to adapt to the consequent human-AI interactive effects of this technology. Thus, my impetus tends towards supporting human (and beyond-human) agency and situating the current moment within historical trends and broader narratives of inequality and power. Through my work I want to be prepared such that, should policy discussions or institutional calls for guidance emerge, we are ready to offer evidence-based recommendations grounded in research and practice.

For me, a good collaborative relationship is grounded in mutual respect, intellectual openness, and shared reflection rather than extractive participation. I value collaborators who are willing to engage in dialogue, question assumptions, and bring their lived or professional expertise into the process as co-thinkers rather than subjects.
Because my work involves communities that are often over-researched but under-heard, I particularly need: ethical and respectful engagement practices; patience with iterative, participatory processes; willingness to sit with ambiguity and “wicked” problems; transparency about goals, expectations, and constraints.
I also value interdisciplinary collaboration, especially with people who can challenge my perspective from clinical, social, technical, or lived-experience standpoints. Ultimately, I am seeking collaborators who are interested not just in building technologies, but in rethinking the systems of power, authorization, and participation that shape how technologies come into being.
